fullName: PtychoProbe – Ptychography and X-ray Fluorescence Nanoprobe beamline (33-ID-C)

status2026.detail: PtychoProbe was the last APS-U feature beamline to be installed. First light was projected for October 2025 and in October 2025 the APS announced that PtychoProbe had moved into commissioning; in November 2025 the endstation instrument was still being installed. On the APS Beamline Commissioning Progress chart the station is listed as '33-ID-C: PTYCHO' at stage 3 ('Ops Commissioning' – the chart gives no further definition; in the APS-U commissioning sequence this covers shielding verification/first light) on 26 Jan 2026 and at stage 4 (Technical commissioning) on 5 Oct 2026; it has not yet reached stage 5 (scientific commissioning/early experiments) or 6 (general users). The Beamline Directory lists status 'Commissioning'. A 2026 APS March Meeting abstract (read only via a search-engine summary) described a 5–30 keV beam 'focused to sub-10 nm' and anticipated user availability in mid-2026 and the Aug 2025 schedule expected general users mid-2026 – so the beamline is running a few months behind those projections. 33-ID-C already appears in the APS General User proposal beamline list (page dated 7 Oct 2026). The late-January 2026 update said the APS-U work was 'essentially completed, with all scope delivered' with the final DOE review still pending; DOE's final approval (formal project completion, after CD-4 review in late Sept 2025) was announced on 5 Feb 2026, and all feature beamlines met their Key Performance Parameters (source brightness at a defined energy, usable energy range). The 2026 Directory lists a focused beam of 0.02 × 0.02 µm (20 nm), i.e. the 5 nm design goal is not yet claimed as delivered.

tagline: An X-ray microscope chasing 5-nanometre beams to reveal which elements sit where inside chips, batteries and cells.
summary: PtychoProbe is a new X-ray microscope at the end of a 78-metre beamline in Sector 33 of Argonne's Advanced Photon Source (APS). It aims to focus hard X-rays (5–30 keV) to a spot 5 nanometres wide, about two strands of DNA side by side, and sweep it across a sample. Wherever the beam lands, atoms emit X-rays at energies characteristic of their element (fluorescence), mapping where each element sits, with a design sensitivity of a few atoms. Meanwhile a fast camera records how the beam scatters; because neighbouring spots overlap, a computer can reconstruct an image sharper than the beam itself (ptychography), aiming toward 1 nm on samples that can take the dose. X-rays pass through solid matter, so chips, batteries, catalysts or cement can be imaged intact, and in 3D. In October 2026 it is in technical commissioning, with a 20 nm focus listed so far.

whatAPSUEnables.text: A lens can focus X-rays to the smallest possible spot only if the light is coherent, its waves in step across the lens; otherwise the spot is limited by the shrunken image of the source. Before the upgrade, nanoprobes got coherent light by closing slits: at 2-ID-D, high-resolution work threw away about 90% of the flux. The new ring's electron beam is about 19 times narrower horizontally (14.5 µm root-mean-square width in the nominal flat-beam model instead of 275 µm), so at 8 keV the coherent fraction rises from about 0.08% to about 12%, and the coherent flux by more than 100 times. That lets the finest X-ray lenses, 5 nm-class zone plates and multilayer Laue lenses, be filled with coherent light, which ptychography also needs. The design projects about 1,000 times more photons per square nanometre in the focus, and scans up to 1,000 times faster. The caveat: these projections assumed two undulators; only one is installed, and the focus listed in 2026 is 20 nm.
quantitative: Horizontal electron source size: σx ≈ 275 µm (old APS) → 14.5 µm (APS-U, 10% coupling), ~19× smaller; APS-U flat-beam ID source σx = 14.5 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.1 µm, σy' = 1.29 µrad, εx = 39.7 pm·rad
Coherent fraction at 8 keV for a 4.8 m undulator: ~0.08% (old lattice) → ~11.6% (MBA)
Coherent flux increase of more than two orders of magnitude vs the pre-upgrade APS
Focused flux density: ~10⁵–10⁶ ph/s/0.01%BW/nm² for a 50 nm spot before the upgrade → ~10⁸–10⁹ ph/s/0.01%BW/nm² for a 5 nm spot after (projection)
Pre-upgrade 2-ID-D high-resolution mode used ~80 µm horizontal slits, sacrificing ~90% of the flux
FDR prediction at SSA1 with slits opened to the coherence length: 5.1 × 10¹² ph/s coherent (Si(111), 10 keV), 7.5 × 10¹¹ ph/s (Si(311), 10 keV), 2.5 × 10¹¹ ph/s (Si(111), 25 keV)
FDR prediction at focus: 3.1 × 10¹⁰ ph/s in a 4 × 4 nm² FWHM spot (4 nm-zone ZP, Si(311), 10 keV); 1.8 × 10¹¹ ph/s in 10 × 10 nm² (16 nm ZP, Si(111), 10 keV)
Scans 'a thousand times faster' than pre-upgrade APS beamlines; sample scan rates up to 1,000× faster
Projected raw data: ~48.8 PB/year (4.8 PB compressed) vs ~0.73 PB/year today across 2-ID-D ptychography, 2-ID-E and BNP XRF (the document calls this ~100×; straight division gives ~67×)

techniques.name: Scanning X-ray fluorescence nanoprobe microscopy
techniques.text: The focused beam knocks inner electrons out of atoms; as each atom recovers it emits X-rays at energies characteristic of its element, a fingerprint called X-ray fluorescence (XRF). An energy-resolving silicon drift detector beside the sample sorts these by energy at every scan point, building maps of where each element sits; with a 5 nm probe the projected sensitivity is a few zinc atoms in a sample a few micrometres thick. It looks in at 90° to the beam, as close as possible; at 90° within the plane of the beam's horizontal polarization, scattered background is weakest. Excitation up to 30 keV reaches the K edges of elements up to tin and the L or M lines of heavier ones. Because a 5 nm focus stays sharp over only ±0.3 µm in depth at 10 keV, maps of thicker samples are projections; true 3D needs fluorescence tomography.

techniques.name: Ptychography (scanning coherent diffraction imaging)
techniques.text: Ptychography makes an image without relying on a perfect lens. A coherent beam is scanned across the sample in overlapping steps, typically overlapping by 60–70%, while a pixel detector records the far-field diffraction pattern at each; algorithms then recover the sample's transmission, in amplitude and phase, and the shape of the beam itself, consistent with all the patterns at once. Resolution is set by how far out the detector still catches scattered photons, not by the spot size. That signal falls steeply with scattering angle (roughly as its inverse fourth power), so each tenfold gain in resolution costs about 10,000 times more dose, and the ultimate limit is how much radiation the sample can take. Scanning continuously ('fly scanning') instead of stop-and-go saves time; the Velociprobe, a prototype instrument built at the APS, reached 8.8 nm on a gold test pattern this way.

techniques.name: Ptychographic and fluorescence tomography (3D nano-imaging)
techniques.text: Rotating the sample and repeating the scan from hundreds of angles lets a computer assemble a 3D volume, as in a hospital CT scan, but for samples at most 3 mm across, at nanometre detail. Both the ptychographic and the fluorescence signals can be used this way. For 5 nm tomography the rotation must be known to about 40 µrad (0.0023°), and a rotating sample must still be tracked to about a nanometre, which the design addresses with anti-rotation references, tracking interferometers or rotating references read by capacitive sensors. For comparison, ptychographic X-ray tomography of a 7 nm-node chip at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) reached 4 nm in 2024.

techniques.name: Spectro-microscopy / chemical-state mapping
techniques.text: By stepping the X-ray energy across an element's absorption edge, the energy at which it suddenly absorbs strongly, the microscope can tell, for example, rusted iron from metallic iron: not only where an element is, but in what chemical form. The silicon monochromator sets the energy to about one part in 7,000. A zone plate's focal length is proportional to the X-ray energy, so the lens has to move to keep focus as the energy changes. Superconducting emission spectrometers with about 1 eV resolution could one day give the chemical form from a single scan, but they depend on detectors still in development.

techniques.name: Simultaneous multimodal XRF + ptychography
techniques.text: Both signals are recorded in the same scan: ptychography shows the shape and density of structures, fluorescence shows what they are made of, in two perfectly registered maps. The beam profile recovered by ptychography can be used to sharpen the fluorescence maps beyond the probe size, and the phase image supplies the mass and density that make fluorescence quantitative. With fast scanning, large areas can be surveyed coarsely and regions of interest then re-scanned at the highest resolution. The beamline directory lists this simultaneous mode as PtychoProbe's special capability.

scienceCases.title: Looking inside computer chips without cutting them open
scienceCases.text: Chips now have features only a few nanometres across. PtychoProbe aims to image their 3D wiring and to map dopant atoms, impurities and chemical states inside intact devices, a non-destructive CT scan for microelectronics. Targets include contact interfaces, thickness variations of hafnium-oxide gate insulators, diffusion barriers, and electromigration, in which the current drags metal atoms along. Benchmarks set elsewhere include 4 nm ptychographic tomography of a 7 nm-node chip at the Paul Scherrer Institute in 2024, and real-time reconstruction by artificial intelligence of data streamed at up to 2 kHz at the Advanced Photon Source's Hard X-ray Nanoprobe, on a test pattern rather than a chip. Dedicated 3D chip imaging toward and below the 5 nm node is also planned for the LYNX instrument at 31-ID-E, complementary to PtychoProbe.

scienceCases.title: Batteries, fuel cells and electrolyzers at the nanoscale
scienceCases.text: Batteries, fuel cells and electrolyzers work or fail at interfaces a few nanometres thick. PtychoProbe is designed to map where ions such as calcium sit, and the chemical state of metal atoms, inside integrated devices, thin interfacial films and nanostructured electrodes, including conversion-type electrodes. Ideas presented at the 2023 first-experiments workshop, not all aimed at PtychoProbe itself, ranged from functional phases in fuel cells and water electrolyzers to electrode–electrolyte interfaces and metal films in an electrochemical cell. One limit: a 5 nm zone plate must sit only a few millimetres from the sample, leaving little room for working cells; long-working-distance in situ work is the role of the In Situ Nanoprobe (ISN) at 19-ID, whose mirrors focus 61 mm away.

scienceCases.title: Single catalyst particles in 3D
scienceCases.text: About 90% of chemical products are made with catalysts. Seeing the size, shape and chemistry of individual catalyst nanoparticles inside a real, millimetre-sized pellet, including how each particle interacts with its support, helps chemists design better ones. Noble-metal catalysts such as ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, silver, platinum and gold need hard X-rays to reach their absorption edges. PtychoProbe aims at 3D chemical imaging down to 5 nm with fluorescence, and finer with ptychography.

scienceCases.title: Stronger, greener concrete for roads and bridges
scienceCases.text: Concrete fails because tiny defects grow into cracks, and making Portland cement emits about 5% of the world's CO₂. Imaging how cement grains react, harden and deteriorate at 5 nm could lead to longer-lasting, lower-carbon roads and bridges. Earlier work at the Advanced Photon Source combined nano-tomography and nano-fluorescence to measure the 3D structure, chemistry and density of hydrating grains of tricalcium silicate, the main ingredient of cement, during the quiet 'induction period' early in hydration.

scienceCases.title: Mapping the brain's wiring and the chemistry of cells
scienceCases.text: Hard X-rays can see through a whole block of brain tissue, so neurons could be traced in 3D without cutting it into thin slices. The goal is imaging below 10 nm over volumes of 100 µm³ and more; a cubic millimetre at 10 nm voxels would be about a petabyte of data. Radiation damage limits frozen, hydrated biological samples to about 10 nm, so PtychoProbe concentrates on more radiation-hard samples. A forerunner, the Bionanoprobe at the Advanced Photon Source, combined 3D fluorescence and ptychographic tomography of whole frozen cells of the green alga Chlamydomonas, mapping metals inside single cells.

scienceCases.title: Dust from space and the chemistry of our environment
scienceCases.text: Micrometeorites and comet dust are made of nanoscale grains that record the birth of the Solar System, and soils and ashes hide toxic or valuable metals in nanoparticles. PtychoProbe can measure the elemental make-up and chemical form of the nanoscale parts of micrometeorites about 10 µm across, follow how microbes and minerals control the chemistry of contaminants, and trace metals through phytoplankton. Workshop proposals also covered the resource potential and risks of coal-ash waste, and thin-film solar cells including perovskites.

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#3 revolver – 2.1 cm magnet structure (APS21#8, table row 'DS-1')
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (one of two structures on a rotating strongback)
insertionDevices.notes: Device sits in the downstream (DS) position of the Sector 33 straight; the upstream (US) position is empty (Sep 2026). In the table 'DS-1' and 'DS-2' denote this device's two magnet structures (APS21#8 and APS25#6), not two positions. Device design minimum gap 8.5 mm (table note 7), current admin/user minimum gap 8.9 mm (row partly garbled); K_eff 1.38 and E1 = 8.34 keV at 8.5 mm; 216 kW/mrad², 5.4 kW at 200 mA. Period count is garbled in the S33 table row; identical APS21R25 devices at S08/S09 have 112 periods → ~2.35 m (inferred). FDR Table 4.47 uses K = 1.305 (E1 = 8.8 keV) for U21.

source.canting: None – single in-line source on the straight-section axis (no canting magnets). FDR planned two in-line revolvers with a phase shifter; as of Sep 2026 only the downstream position is filled.
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High-Heat-Load Front End (HHLFE; designed for two in-line undulators, 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad² peak) in windowless configuration with a built-in differential pump. Sequence (FDR Fig. 3.2): lead-lined photon shutter LPPS, storage-ring valve, BTFM1 burn-through mask, fixed masks FM2/FM3, collimator, GRID-XBPM (XBPM1), photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor IM1, safety shutters SS1&SS2, wall collimator in the ratchet wall, FE valve, exit mask with XBPM2 (2 × 2 mm, 25.4 m) and tungsten exit collimator (5 × 5 mm, 26.1 m, narrowed to manage bremsstrahlung for small-offset monochromators), beamline isolation valve. The FE exit table sits inside 33-ID-A. A residual gas analyser is required in the FOE for windowless operation.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at an ID straight (Aug 2024): flat-beam mode (κ = 0.1) σx = 14.5 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm, σy' = 1.29 µrad (εx = 39.7 pm·rad, εy = 4.0 pm·rad); round-beam mode (κ = 1) σx = 12.3 µm, σx' = 2.34 µrad, σy = 8.26 µm, σy' = 3.47 µrad (ε = 28.7 pm·rad each); natural emittance 41.5 pm·rad. Single-electron photon contribution for L ≈ 2.35 m at 10 keV (calculated, σr = √(2λL)/4π ≈ 1.9 µm, σr' = √(λ/2L) ≈ 5.1 µrad) gives total photon source ≈ 14.6 × 3.6 µm and 5.8 × 5.3 µrad (flat beam, estimate). Horizontal source ~4.7× larger than vertical in flat mode – one reason the beamline uses horizontally deflecting optics for stability. FDR calculations used Borland's Oct 2018 CD-2 source parameters. Gaussian-beam estimate of what the single 2.35 m device means relative to the FDR's 4.6 m source (flat beam, 5–25 keV): central-cone flux ×~0.5, brightness/coherent flux ×~0.34 (shorter device = larger photon divergence and worse beta matching) (calculated).

branches.name: 33-ID PtychoProbe (single in-line beamline)
branches.description: One beam path: HHL front end → first optics enclosure 33-ID-A (slits, M1, DCM, [DMM], M2, masks) → shielded transport → 33-ID-B (SSA/BDA1, pink/mono shutters) → shielded transport through mini-hutches → 33-ID-C (SSA/BDA2, PtychoProbe vacuum instrument, 5.6 m in-vacuum detector mover, beam stop). Two optical modes are selected by refocusing the bendable mirrors: image the source on SSA1 at 47.9 m ('best focus', ~22 m to the lens) or on SSA2 at 57.8 m ('flux vs resolution', ~12 m to the lens). Pink-beam rated masks/shutters/beam stop allow mirror-only or multilayer (pink) operation per FDR.

components.name: Revolver undulator APS21R25#3 (2.1 cm / 2.5 cm periods)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. The device occupies the downstream half of the straight section (ID vacuum chamber 5.363 m flange to flange, nominally 4.8 m of undulator space; FDR Fig. 3.10 and Sec. 3-3.2; position from the APS ID table). Its centre is estimated at about +1.3 m from the straight-section centre, from which FDR distances are measured. The FDR baseline (4.6 m) was centred on the straight.
components.text: A 2.35-metre row of magnets that makes the 6 GeV electrons wiggle and emit an intense, narrow X-ray beam. It is a 'revolver': two magnet arrays with different spacings (2.1 and 2.5 cm) share one support, and opening the gap and rotating it swaps them. The 2.5 cm array's lowest (first-harmonic) energy is 4.6 keV at the device's smallest gap, and with higher harmonics the pair covers 5–30 keV. Only this one device, in the downstream half of the straight, is installed; the design assumed two in a row (4.6 m).

components.name: Front-end GRID X-ray beam position monitor (XBPM1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate and generic: the high-heat-load front-end component order follows FDR Fig. 3.2. No 33-ID-specific position is published; the value is a placeholder for the model.
components.text: An early-warning sensor in the front end that measures exactly where the X-ray beam points, so the accelerator can hold it steady to a few micrometres. This grazing-incidence (GRID) monitor works with two others further along; its position in the model is a generic placeholder.

components.name: Front-end photon shutter PS2 and safety shutters SS1/SS2
components.distanceNote: Approximate and generic: order from FDR Fig. 3.2, just upstream of the ratchet wall. No 33-ID-specific value is published.
components.text: Heavy doors for the beam: a water-cooled photon shutter absorbs the beam's heat, and two independent tungsten safety shutters behind it block high-energy radiation, so people can safely enter the hutches. All three are interlocked with the personnel safety system.

components.name: Storage-ring shield (ratchet) wall with wall collimator
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the FOE upstream wall is at ~23.6 m on the FDR Fig. 4.31 plan; the wall thickness is taken to be similar to other sectors (~1.5 m).
components.text: The thick concrete shield wall between the accelerator tunnel and the experiment hall. The beam passes through a small opening lined with a metal collimator, so radiation cannot stream out alongside it. Its position and thickness here are estimates.

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2 (2 × 2 mm)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.
components.text: A water-cooled metal block with a 2 × 2 mm hole: only the bright central core of the beam enters the beamline, and the rest is absorbed here as heat. A built-in beam-position monitor checks the pointing. There is no beryllium window; differential pumping separates the beamline's vacuum from the ring's.

components.name: Front-end tungsten exit collimator (5 × 5 mm)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.
components.text: A thick tungsten block with a 5 × 5 mm hole that stops bremsstrahlung, very high-energy radiation made when electrons hit residual gas in the ring, except in a narrow pencil around the beam. The upgrade narrowed it so that beamlines whose monochromators shift the beam only slightly can manage this radiation.

components.name: HHL white-beam slits 33ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.
components.text: Adjustable tungsten-edged jaws that trim the raw beam before it reaches the first mirror, sparing the mirror unnecessary heat. Design studies used openings of 2 × 2 mm and 0.5 × 0.5 mm.

components.name: M1 high-heat-load horizontal focusing mirror
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 elevation drawing labels M1 at ~28.2 m.
components.text: The first optic: a super-smooth silicon mirror met at a grazing angle of 2.5 mrad, about a seventh of a degree. It absorbs much of the heat (about 330–450 W), steers the beam sideways and, being bendable, focuses it horizontally onto a micrometre-sized aperture 20–30 m downstream. The bending also cancels the bump that heat raises on the mirror, keeping slope errors, tiny tilts of the surface away from its ideal shape, below 0.1 µrad; stripes of silicon, rhodium and platinum are chosen to reject higher harmonics, X-rays at multiples of the chosen energy.

components.name: Secondary scattering collimator 33ID-SC-1 (lead)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.
components.text: Lead shielding just after the first mirror that catches X-rays scattered by it. It deals with scattered rather than direct radiation, hence the name 'secondary' collimator.

components.name: Photon mask 33ID-PM-1 (pink-beam mis-steering mask)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.
components.text: A safety mask just after the first mirror. It catches the mirror-reflected ('pink') beam if that is ever steered the wrong way.

components.name: Beam diagnostic 33ID-BD-1 (BPM / fluorescent flag)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.

components.name: Horizontal double-crystal monochromator 33ID-MN-1
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 drawing shows the 'DCM' at ~30.5 m.
components.text: Two perfect silicon crystals pick out a single X-ray energy, to about one part in 7,000. They deflect the beam sideways rather than up and down, because floor vibrations are much smaller horizontally and the source is wider in that direction, so a small wobble matters less. Because the undulator light is horizontally polarized, a sideways reflection loses some intensity (π geometry): about 70% of an up-down reflection's throughput at 6 keV, over 90% above 10 keV. The crystals are cooled with liquid nitrogen; whether a narrower-band Si(311) pair was also installed is unconfirmed.

specs.crystals: Si(111) (FDR spec text: 'standard Si(111)'; Si(311) only in FDR calculations; unconfirmed)
specs.Throughput in π geometry: ≈70% of σ at 6 keV; >90% above 10 keV (Si 111)

components.name: Double-multilayer monochromator 33ID-MN-2 (FDR baseline; installation unconfirmed)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39. It is neither labelled on the 2024 elevation drawing nor listed in the 2026 directory, so it is drawn as a translucent ghost.
components.text: An optional high-flux monochromator from the design, built from hundreds of alternating nanometre-thin layers of molybdenum and boron carbide. It passes a much wider band of energies, tens of times more light, for fast ptychography where perfect energy purity is not needed. Its installation is not confirmed, so the model shows it as a ghost; the Velociprobe, PtychoProbe's prototype at 2-ID-D, used one for fly-scan ptychography at 3,000 frames a second.

components.name: M2 vertical focusing mirror
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 drawing shows 'M2' at ~33.0 m.
components.text: A second bendable mirror, deflecting vertically, that focuses the beam up and down onto the same aperture as the first mirror and helps strip away unwanted higher-energy X-rays. Its slope error is below 0.05 µrad. Together, the two mirrors steer the useful beam off the straight-through line, so stops downstream can catch the raw beam and bremsstrahlung.

components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.

components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.

components.name: Shielded transport 33ID-ST-1 (pink/mono)
components.distanceNote: Runs from 35.7 to 41.5 m (FDR Table 4.39). The 2024 drawing shows mini-hutch 33-ID-A-MH-1 on this run at ~39.3–40.6 m. The marker is drawn at mid-span.

components.name: Secondary-source aperture SSA1 / beam-defining aperture BDA1 (33ID-SL-2) with BPM
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; labelled 'BDA1' at ~47.5–48 m on the 2024 drawing.
components.text: A pair of slits a few micrometres apart, far narrower than a hair, that becomes the new 'source' the microscope's lens images. Opened to about 4.8 µm, a width set by the wavelength, the distance and the lens size, it passes only light that is coherent across the lens, and it turns wobbles of the mirrors upstream into slight brightness flicker rather than a moving spot. Water-cooled, with tungsten blades, it can be positioned to 100 nm. This 'best focus' position is 22 m from the lens.

specs.blades: Glidcop faces at ≤5° incidence, tungsten defining blades

components.name: Photon mask 33ID-PM-3 (pink-beam mask)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39.

components.name: Tungsten mono shutter 33ID-SH-2

components.name: Shielded transport 33ID-ST-2 (pink/mono)
components.distanceNote: Runs from 51.8 to 57.5 m (FDR Table 4.39), passing mini-hutches 33-ID-B-MH-1 (~53.0–54.3 m) and 33-ID-C-MH-1 (~56.0–57.4 m) on the 2024 drawing. The marker is drawn at mid-span.

components.name: Secondary-source aperture SSA2 / BDA2 (33ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 drawing places the BDA2 assembly at ~57.5–59 m.
components.text: An alternative secondary source, 10 metres closer to the microscope and about 12 m from the lens. The design calls it the 'flux versus resolution' position: it trades some sharpness for more light, or the reverse, depending on how far it is opened. It has the same water cooling, ±50 µm travel and 100 nm positioning as the first one.

components.name: Nanofocusing optics: Fresnel zone plates and multilayer Laue lenses
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the optic sits one focal length (5.8–23 mm, FDR Table 4.45) upstream of the sample at 69.7 m. It is drawn ~10 mm upstream of the sample, between the two design focal lengths, and enlarged for visibility.
components.text: The microscope's objective lens, which focuses the beam to a few nanometres. A Fresnel zone plate is a disc of thousands of concentric, nanometre-thin metal rings, typically gold, that bends X-rays by diffraction into a focus; multilayer Laue lenses are thin slices cut from a stack of nanometre layers and focus in one direction each. The finest ring sets the spot: an ideal 5 nm zone plate for 10 keV has 4 nm outer rings, 11,250 zones, a 180 µm diameter and a focal length of just 5.8 mm. Because the focus moves with energy, the lenses ride on a gantry; four zone plates cover 5–30 keV, and the Laue lenses are preferred above 13 keV. The real optic, under 0.2 mm across, is shown much enlarged.

specs.ideal5nmZP_10keV: Δr 4 nm, D 180 µm, f 5.8 mm, N 11250
specs.chromaticLimit: λ/Δλ ≥ N zones: Si(111) (≈7,100) suffices for the 16 nm ZP at 10 keV and the 4 nm ZP at 25 keV, not for the 4 nm ZP at 10 keV

components.name: Order-sorting aperture and central stop
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the zone plate and the sample, a few millimetres upstream of the sample.
components.text: A zone plate sends light into several diffraction orders, not only the focus. A small central stop on the lens blocks the unfocused straight-through beam, and a tiny pinhole just before the sample, the order-sorting aperture, passes only the first-order focus.

specs.heritageExample: Velociprobe: 60 µm W central stop, 30 µm OSA ~62 mm downstream of a 50 nm-zone ZP

components.name: Optics-to-sample laser-interferometer metrology
components.distanceNote: At the instrument. Drawn as interferometer heads on the chamber with beams to the optics module and the sample stage; the layout is illustrative.
components.text: Laser interferometers and capacitive sensors keep measuring where the lens and the sample are, to about a nanometre, so every pixel of the image is placed correctly even while the sample moves. The design asks for 0.5–1 nm relative accuracy. The Velociprobe prototype logged six interferometer axes 25,000 times a second for the same purpose.

components.name: PtychoProbe endstation instrument 33ID-BI-1 (granite air-bearing nanopositioning stack in vacuum chamber)
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 drawing shows the 'Ptycho Endstation' at ~69.3–70.6 m.
components.text: The heart of the beamline: a vacuum chamber holding lens and sample on a stack of massive granite blocks. While being positioned the blocks float on thin air cushions; then the air is vented and they settle granite on granite, solid as rock. About 26 motorized axes move the optics on a gantry and the sample on coarse, rotation and fast scanning stages, and the vertical stage is a pair of granite wedges. Samples up to 10 × 10 mm (2D) or 3 mm across (3D) can be swept through the beam at up to 7 mm per second and still be placed to better than 2.5 nm, in vacuum or in helium, nitrogen, argon or air.

components.name: Energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: At the sample, at 90° to the beam (FDR). The horizontal plane is inferred from the horizontal polarization and is not documented. Drawn on the outboard side, entering a side port of the chamber; the actual side (inboard or outboard) is not documented.
components.text: A silicon drift detector beside the sample, at right angles to the beam, that sorts incoming X-rays by energy to tell which elements are glowing and how much of each is there. At 90° in the plane of the beam's polarization, scattered background is weakest. A seven-element detector reading full spectra 1,000 times a second was planned in 2024; the directory lists an 'energy dispersive detector'.

components.name: In-vacuum detector mover / flight tube (IRELEC, 5.6 m)
components.distanceNote: Approximate start: the fast detector can sit 75 mm from the sample, so the tank couples directly to the instrument chamber. The FDR flight tube runs from 70.0 to 76.5 m; the 2024 drawing shows the 'Detector Mover' tank at ~70.6–76.7 m. Drawn as on the 2024 drawing: coupling and gate valve at ~70.4 m, tank ~70.55–76.6 m and ~0.76 m in diameter (scaled from the elevation and plan), with rails reaching through the coupling to the instrument.
components.text: A 5.6-metre vacuum tank, longer than a car, inside which two X-ray cameras ride on rails. The fast one can sit just 75 mm behind the sample to catch widely scattered X-rays from the smallest beams, and the large one can back off to 5 m. The distance sets the size of the reconstructed pixels, and with no air in the way the faint scattered X-rays are neither absorbed nor drowned in air scatter.

components.name: Fast photon-counting detector (DECTRIS SELUN)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: as close as 75 mm from the sample, travelling inside the detector mover. Drawn at that closest documented position, reached through the coupling into the instrument chamber. Both detectors are shown at the ends of their travel, although only one is in the beam at a time.
components.text: A small, ultra-fast photon-counting camera: 190 × 190 pixels of 100 µm, taking up to 30,000 frames a second (120,000 with pixels binned 2 × 2). It works close to the sample, in vacuum, to record the widely scattered X-rays from the smallest beams. Its maker specifies the silicon sensor for 8–30 keV, so how the 5–8 keV end of the range is covered is not documented.

components.name: Large photon-counting detector (DECTRIS EIGER2 XE 1.5M)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: up to 5 m from the sample; the FDR lists detector 33ID-DT-1 at 75.3 m. Drawn at its farthest documented position, 5 m from the sample.
components.text: A larger photon-counting camera with 75 µm pixels that can move up to 5 m back, so the diffraction pattern from larger beams spreads out and its fine detail can be recorded. It takes up to 2,000 frames a second, about 6 GB of raw data every second.

components.name: Pink-beam stop 33ID-BS-1
components.distanceNote: Design position from FDR Table 4.39; the 2024 drawing shows it at ~77.3 m, at the downstream wall.
components.text: The end of the line: a heavy block at the downstream wall of 33-ID-C that safely absorbs whatever beam is left, rated even for the mirror-reflected ('pink') beam.

instruments.name: PtychoProbe endstation (scanning X-ray nanoprobe + ptychography microscope)
instruments.text: A vacuum-chamber microscope on air-bearing granite blocks. A zone plate or multilayer Laue lens focuses the beam, and the sample is swept through it at up to 7 mm per second while interferometers track optic and sample to about 1 nm, a fluorescence detector reads the elements and a pixel camera records the scattering; the sample can be rotated ±180° for 3D. During the scan, real-time control corrects positions by feedback and feed-forward, triggers the detectors and makes quick low-resolution reconstructions. A small set of sample environments (cooling, a flow cell, electrical connections) was planned, but none is confirmed as built.
detectors: Energy-dispersive silicon drift detector at ~90° (Vortex ME7 planned)
sampleEnvironments: Helium, nitrogen, argon or air atmosphere
Planned in the FDR: sample cooling, flow cell, electrical connections (not confirmed as built)

instruments.name: In-vacuum detector mover (5.6 m flight tube with two detectors)
instruments.text: A long vacuum tank behind the microscope, built by IRELEC, in which two cameras glide on rails: a fast one as close as 75 mm for the smallest beams, a large one as far as 5 m for larger ones. Keeping the whole flight path in vacuum removes air absorption and scatter from the faint, widely scattered signal that sets the resolution of ptychography, toward the 1 nm goal.

instruments.name: VelociProbe (listed by the APS Directory at 33-ID-C; status unclear)
instruments.text: The fast-scanning ptychography prototype built at the APS and installed at 2-ID-D, whose granite, air-bearing and laser-tracking ideas PtychoProbe inherits. It logged six interferometer axes 25,000 times a second; accelerometers showed its granite optics gantry and sample stage vibrating relative to each other by only 0.75–1.4 nm (root-mean-square, 5–100 Hz). It reached 8.8 nm resolution on a gold test pattern and about 10 nm on a chip at 3,000 frames per second. The 2026 directory lists a VelociProbe endstation at 33-ID-C, but a move from 2-ID-D is not otherwise documented.

geometryNotes:
PtychoProbe is a single straight-through beamline with no canting: one revolver undulator in the downstream half of the Sector 33 straight feeds a windowless HHL front end; the FE exit table is inside 33-ID-A.

Optics are all in 33-ID-A (23.6–36.0 m): M1 deflects horizontally by 5 mrad (2 × 2.5 mrad) at 28.3 m, the DCM (and FDR DMM) add only a ~1 mm horizontal offset, and M2 deflects vertically by 5 mrad at 33.1 m. Consequently the optical axis walks off the source axis by ≈ 34 mm horizontally and ≈ 10 mm vertically at the FOE exit (35 m) and by ≈ 0.21 m horizontally and ≈ 0.18 m vertically at the sample (69.7 m) – calculated from FDR distances; the inboard/outboard and up/down senses are not documented, so this exhibit keeps the axis straight, as the published drawings do.

Downstream hutches are in-line: 33-ID-B (41.2–52.1 m, ~1.7 m wide) holds SSA1; 33-ID-C (57.4–77.6 m, ~4 m wide) holds SSA2 at its entrance, then ~12 m of empty transport, the PtychoProbe instrument at ~69.7 m and the 5.6 m detector-mover tank to ~76.7 m, with the beam stop at the end wall. Shielded transport pipes connect hutches, passing three small mini-hutches (A-MH-1, B-MH-1, C-MH-1) on the 2024 drawing.

On the FDR plan 33-BM-B/C hutches sit on the inboard side of the ID line, and the 33-ID-C control room and vestibule run along the inboard wall; the hutches of the neighbouring sector appear at an angle on the outboard side.

Beam height: 1.400 m above floor at the ID straight (FDR Fig. 3.10); hall beam height at 33-ID is not published, and M2's 5 mrad vertical deflection shifts it by ~0.18 m (up or down, unknown) at the sample.

Distances: FDR (2019) values are measured from the straight-section centre; the 2024 elevation drawing (a late-design drawing published before the instrument was installed in Nov 2025, not an as-built record) agrees with the FDR to within ~0.5 m except that the BDA2 assembly appears at ~57.5–59 m and the detector mover spans ~70.6–76.7 m.

Exhibit model: the beam axis is kept straight (as in all published drawings) because the deflection senses of M1 and M2 are undocumented; hutch outlines (stepped, tapering 33-ID-A; chamfered 33-ID-C; control room from ~54.4 m), mini-hutch heights, the instrument stack and the detector-mover tank are scaled from FDR Figs. 4.31/4.37 and the 2024 elevation drawing (±0.2 m); the zone plate, OSA and crystal offsets are enlarged for visibility.

interactiveIdeas.title: Make the light march in step: the secondary-source aperture
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors see the source image projected by M1/M2 onto SSA1 and a slit they can close with a slider. Beside it: the zone plate's focal spot (live convolution of the demagnified slit with the lens's Airy pattern) and a flux meter. A toggle swaps the old APS source (275 µm wide) for the APS-U source (14.5 µm). With the old source the visitor must close the slit until almost all the light is lost to get a sharp spot; with APS-U a sharp spot keeps most of the light.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why nanoprobes are brightness-limited, what 'coherent' means in practice, and why the upgrade was transformative for this beamline.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot s = √(s_demag² + s_diff²) (PDR); s_demag = Δ·(f/z) with z ≈ 21.8 m (SSA1→lens) or ~12 m (SSA2), f = 5.8 mm (5 nm ZP at 10 keV) - demagnification ~3,800×; diffraction spot ≈ 1.22·Δr_N (Rayleigh) or ~Δr_N FWHM; coherent filling of a lens of diameter D needs Δ ≲ λz/(πD) = 4.82 µm (FDR). Source image at SSA1 from FDR distances: horizontal magnification ≈ 0.69, vertical ≈ 0.45 (calculated), so at 10 keV flat beam the image is ~24 µm × ~4 µm FWHM - the slit cuts mostly horizontally. Transmitted flux ∝ ∫Gaussian over the slit; coherent flux saturates once Δ exceeds the coherence length (2.9 × 3.0 µm at 10 keV). Slit vibration of 10% of the opening moves the focus by 10% of the spot (PDR). Old lattice: σx = 275 µm, σx' = 11 µrad; APS-U σx = 14.5 µm.

interactiveIdeas.title: Design your own zone plate
interactiveIdeas.concept: Sliders for X-ray energy (5-30 keV), outermost zone width (4-60 nm) and diameter (50-250 µm) redraw a zone plate (with true ring count shown as a number and a zoomable sector), its focal length, focal spot, depth of focus and how 'pure' the X-ray colour must be. A monochromator switch (Si(111) vs Si(311)) turns the focus red when the bandwidth is too wide. Preset buttons load the FDR 5 nm and 20 nm designs.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a lens made of rings works, why 5 nm lenses are so hard to make, and why the monochromator crystal choice matters for the smallest spots.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: λ[nm] = 1.23984/E[keV]; f = D·Δr_N/λ; number of zones N = D/(4Δr_N); NA = λ/(2Δr_N); resolution ≈ 1.22·Δr_N; depth of focus ±2Δr_N²/λ; chromatic requirement λ/Δλ ≥ N. Check against FDR Table 4.45: 10 keV, 4 nm, 180 µm → f = 5.8 mm, N = 11,250; 25 keV, 72 µm → f = 5.81 mm, N = 4,500. Si(111) ΔE/E ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ (N ≲ 7,000), Si(311) ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵ class - so the 5 nm preset should turn red with Si(111) at 10 keV (N = 11,250) but not at 25 keV (N = 4,500). Efficiency of an ideal binary phase ZP ≤ ~40%; FDR assumes 33% at 1900 nm (10 keV) / 4400 nm (25 keV) thickness - aspect ratios of ~475-1100 are why MLLs (two crossed 1D lenses) and conic/volume zone plates are pursued. Higher diffraction orders need a central stop + order-sorting aperture. Depth of focus for 5 nm at 10 keV is only ±0.3 µm.

interactiveIdeas.title: Seeing finer than the beam: build a ptychography image
interactiveIdeas.concept: A hidden test object (e.g. a chip layout or a cell) is scanned by a glowing probe circle; each position produces a speckle pattern on a virtual detector. The visitor drags the overlap slider and the photon-count slider, then presses 'reconstruct' to watch an in-browser ePIE iterate from noise to an image - and simultaneously recover the probe. With overlap < ~50% or too few photons, the image fails or blurs.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: That the image comes from computation on diffraction data, why overlap and coherence matter, and that resolution is ultimately limited by how many photons you can afford to put on the sample.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Far-field intensity I(q) = |F{P(r − r_j)·O(r)}|²; ePIE updates object and probe alternately; reconstruction pixel Δx = λz/(N·p) (e.g. 10 keV, 155 mm, 512 × 75 µm → 0.5 nm); oversampling in ptychography is relaxed by overlap but each pattern must be sampled finer than the speckle (probe-size) scale; overlap typically 60-70% (step ≲ 0.3-0.4 of probe diameter; FDR uses 66%). Resolution is set by the highest q with adequate SNR, and with Porod-like I ∝ q⁻⁴ a 10× finer resolution needs ~10⁴× more photons - show Poisson noise explicitly. Pitfalls: phase wrapping, global phase/position ambiguities, partial coherence (needs mixed-state probes), position errors (interferometer data), fly-scan blur.

interactiveIdeas.title: Count the atoms: X-ray fluorescence detective
interactiveIdeas.concept: A simulated integrated circuit with copper and tungsten lines and arsenic-doped regions (after PDR Fig. 6.61) is scanned with a 50 nm beam ('old APS nanoprobe') or a 5 nm beam ('PtychoProbe'). An energy spectrum builds up photon by photon; visitors place energy windows on peaks to make element maps, and tune incident energy above/below the As K edge to make arsenic appear or vanish.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How fluorescence fingerprints identify elements, why the incident energy must exceed an absorption edge, and how a smaller, brighter beam reveals features that were averaged away.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Line energies: Cu Kα 8.05 keV (K edge 8.98), Zn Kα 8.64, As Kα 10.54 (K edge 11.87 keV - excitation must exceed it), W Lα 8.40 and Lβ 9.67 keV (L3 edge 10.21), Fe Kα 6.40 keV; overlaps (W Lα near Cu/Zn region; As Kα vs Pb Lα 10.55) must be shown. Counts follow Poisson statistics; detection limit ~3σ above background; signal ∝ flux × dwell × concentration × cross-section × solid angle; 90° geometry in the horizontal plane minimises elastic scatter for horizontally polarized light. 5 nm optics have only ±0.3 µm depth of focus at 10 keV, so thick samples give projections. Projected sensitivity: a few Zn atoms in few-µm samples.

interactiveIdeas.title: The stillness challenge
interactiveIdeas.concept: A 5 nm beam spot sits over a 5 nm feature. Visitors can stomp (floor vibration), open a hutch door (air flow), or nudge a thermostat by 0.1 °C and watch the spot smear and the image blur. Then they 'install' granite stages, air-bearing venting, interferometer feedback and hutch temperature control one by one and see the error budget shrink.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why a nanoprobe is as much a precision-engineering feat as an optics one, and why the beamline uses granite, vacuum, horizontal bounces and lasers.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thermal expansion ΔL = α·L·ΔT: 10 cm of aluminium grows ~230 nm and granite ~60 nm for a 0.1 °C change (PDR); target hutch stability 0.1 °C/24 h and floor background < 20 nm rms (2-100 Hz). Velociprobe relative vibration between the granite optics gantry and the granite sample X axis 1.4 nm rms (X) and 0.75 nm rms (Y) over 5-100 Hz; PtychoProbe fly-scan precision < 2.5 nm, metrology 1 nm. Horizontal deflection is preferred because the horizontal source is larger than the vertical (~4.7× in flat-beam mode, ~1.5× in round-beam mode) (angular errors matter less) and floor vibration is smaller horizontally. The SSA converts upstream optic vibrations into intensity fluctuations rather than spot motion.

interactiveIdeas.title: Fly-scan race and the data flood
interactiveIdeas.concept: A game where the visitor sets scan speed and detector frame rate to cover a whole 1 mm² chip region at 5 nm detail before the 'beamtime clock' runs out. Speeding up blurs each frame unless overlap and frame rate keep up; a data-rate gauge fills a counter of hard drives in real time.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How continuous scanning, fast detectors and computing turn nanometre microscopy from postage stamps into whole devices.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Scan speed v = step × frame rate, step = d_probe·(1 − overlap): 20 nm probe, 66% overlap, 1 MHz → ~6.8 mm/s (FDR's 7 mm/s limit; Directory lists ≤7 mm/s). Frame sizes: EIGER2 XE 1.5M ~3 MB at 2 kHz ≈ 6 GB/s; 200 × 200-pixel fast detector at 30 kHz ≈ 2.4 GB/s; annual raw ≈ 48.8 PB. Velociprobe benchmark: 3 kHz frames, 10 nm resolution, ~9 × 10⁴ resolution elements/s; PSI 2024: 14,000 resolution elements/s at 4 nm. Motion during an exposure is handled with mixed-state (multi-mode) probe reconstruction; detector duty cycle matters (SELUN >98.8%).

interactiveIdeas.title: Why does the monochromator bounce sideways?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two views of the same crystal pair: bouncing up (σ geometry) vs sideways (π geometry) with the undulator's horizontally polarised light. A dial sweeps photon energy; a meter shows relative throughput, and a vibration view shows how much the focus moves for a 0.1 µrad wobble in each orientation.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: That X-ray polarization and source shape drive real engineering choices - here trading a little flux at low energy for stability.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg: λ = 2d·sinθ_B, d(Si 111) = 3.1356 Å, d(Si 311) = 1.6375 Å. π-polarization factor |cos 2θ_B| (dynamical) vanishes at θ_B = 45°: Si(111) at 2.80 keV, Si(311) at 5.35 keV. Two-crystal throughput relative to σ: Si(111) ≈ 0.70 at 6 keV, 0.91 at 10 keV; Si(311) 0.66 at 10 keV. That is why the 2017 PDR asked for a vertically polarized undulator and why the as-built Si(111)-only listing is plausible. Angular jitter δ of a mirror moves the image by 2δ·q; for a two-crystal DCM a common rotation of both crystals leaves the exit direction unchanged, so only the crystal-to-crystal (relative) angle error δrel matters (image shift 2δrel·q); it matters relative to the source size in that plane (flat beam σx ≈ 14.5 µm vs σy ≈ 3.1 µm).

funFacts: The 5 nm zone-plate design for 10 keV has 11,250 concentric rings packed into a disc just 180 µm across – about the width of two human hairs (FDR Table 4.45).

A temperature change of just 0.1 °C makes a 10 cm aluminium part grow 230 nm and a granite part 60 nm – 12 to 46 times the 5 nm goal, which is why the microscope is built from granite and the hutch is temperature-controlled.
The cameras live inside a 5.6-metre-long vacuum tank on rails; one can sit just 75 mm behind the sample, the other can retreat 5 metres.
At 5 nm resolution and 10 keV the beam stays in focus over only about ±0.3 µm – about 1/100 of the width of a human hair – so most real samples are thicker than the focus is 'deep'.
The microscope's granite blocks float on air cushions while moving and then 'land' for granite-to-granite contact; the vertical stage is a pair of granite wedges with a 5.5° design angle.
Before the upgrade, high-resolution work at the 2-ID-D microprobe (Sector 2, on the far side of the ring) threw away about 90% of the X-rays through narrow slits just to get a clean focus.
The undulator is a 'revolver': it carries two magnet arrays with different spacings (2.1 and 2.5 cm) and rotates to swap them, after safely opening its gap.

PtychoProbe is expected to generate about 48.8 petabytes of raw data a year – which the APS describes as roughly 100 times (by straight division ~67 times) the ~0.73 PB a year of the three APS microscopy instruments it builds on.
Imaging one cubic millimetre of brain at 10 nm voxels would produce about a petabyte of data.
PtychoProbe was the last of the APS-U feature beamlines to be installed; the team was still placing the instrument in November 2025.

The APS feature page compares the goal to biology: a DNA strand is 2.5 nm thick, a sheet of paper about 100,000 nm – and the beamline's top resolution target is 5 nm, with ptychography reaching toward 1 nm.

Its prototype, the Velociprobe, kept the granite blocks carrying lens and sample moving relative to each other by only 1.4 nm and 0.75 nm rms (5–100 Hz vibrations), and imaged a gold test pattern at 8.8 nm resolution.

openQuestions: Source: the Sep 2026 ID table shows only ONE revolver (APS21R25#3, downstream position; 'DS-1'/'DS-2' are its two magnet structures) at Sector 33, whereas the FDR baseline was two in-line revolvers (4.6 m). Whether a second device is planned is not documented; the S33 row's period count is garbled (112/94 periods inferred from identical devices at S08/S09/S19/S20). For the as-built source the FDR values are optimistic: central-cone flux by ~2× and brightness/coherent flux (hence focused coherent flux) by ~3× (Gaussian-beam estimate, calculated) – the Directory's 10¹¹ ph/s at 10 keV is consistent with this.

Monochromators: the 2026 Directory lists only a DCM with ΔE/E = 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ (Si(111)); the FDR optics text itself specifies 'a standard Si(111)' HDCM, with Si(311) appearing only in its calculations, and the FDR component table includes a Mo/B₄C double-multilayer monochromator at 31.9 m. The 2024 elevation drawing labels only M1/DCM/M2. Installation of Si(311) crystals and of the DMM is unconfirmed.

Polarization trade-off: the PDR required a vertically polarized undulator for the horizontal DCM; the FDR switched to a standard (horizontally polarized) revolver. How the beamline obtains Si(311)-class bandwidth for 4 nm-zone optics at 5–8 keV (where π-geometry Si(311) reflectivity collapses) is not documented.
Station naming: FDR text says the PtychoProbe 'will be located at 33-ID-D', but its figures and the 2026 Directory use 33-ID-C; we use 33-ID-C.

The Directory also lists a 'VelociProbe' endstation at 33-ID-C (ZP focusing, 5–20 nm ptychography, air-bearing rotation with <50 nm runout), while recent papers place the Velociprobe at 2-ID-D (data mostly pre-upgrade) and the current 2-ID-D listing no longer mentions it. Whether the Velociprobe was relocated to 33-ID-C (e.g. as a commissioning or second instrument) is unconfirmed.

Nanofocusing optics actually in use: the Directory lists a 20 × 20 nm focus in 2026; whether 5 nm-class ZPs or MLLs have been installed/commissioned, and whether conic zone plates (APS Optics LDRD) will be used, is not published.
Mirror details as built (cooling: PDR LN₂ vs FDR notched side-cooling; exact radii; deflection senses inboard/outboard and up/down) are not public; the exhibit represents these details schematically.

XRF detector as built: 2024 plan names a Vortex ME7; the Directory says only 'Energy Dispersive Detector'. FDR/PDR ideas of a backscatter detector, capillary-collimated detector and a superconducting emission spectrometer have no status information.

Sample environments: the FDR lists only possibilities (cooling, flow cell, electrical feedthroughs; vacuum/He/N₂/Ar/air). No cryogenic sample capability for PtychoProbe is confirmed in 2026 sources (cryo is offered at the 2-ID-D Bionanoprobe).

Positions differing between FDR (2019) and the 2024 drawing: BDA2 (57.8 m vs ~57.5–59 m), detector mover (70.0–76.5 vs ~70.6–76.7 m). Unidentified items on the 2024 drawing: a red-outlined box at ~60–61.3 m and a pair of stands 1000 mm apart at ~67–68 m in 33-ID-C; functions of the three mini-hutches.
Front-end component positions (XBPM1, shutters, ratchet wall) are not published for 33-ID; values in the component list are generic placeholders.

Timeline: the APS March Meeting 2026 abstract (read only via search summary) and the Aug 2025 update anticipated users in mid-2026, but the 5 Oct 2026 chart still shows technical commissioning (stage 4). The date of first early-science experiments is unknown.
Performance demonstrated with beam (focus size, coherent flux, ptychographic resolution at 33-ID) has not yet been published as of Oct 2026.
SELUN (Si sensor) is specified by DECTRIS for 8–30 keV (thresholds from 4.6 keV); how ptychography at 5–8 keV is handled (EIGER2 XE, or SELUN below its nominal range) is not documented.
The Directory's VelociProbe entry at 33-ID-C speaks of 'Fresnel zone plate focusing for micron-size beams' – possibly a defocused/large-beam ('ptychography-poly') mode; its meaning is not explained.
